hints: Focus on what type of alcohol can actually be oxidised all the way to a carboxylic acid.
Remember that only a primary alcohol oxidises via an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with the same carbon skeleton.
Compare the mass added in each step, oxidation adds O while hydrolysis of a nitrile replaces the N part with O atoms.
walkthrough:
**Identify alcohol X**

Only a primary alcohol can be oxidised in two stages to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone which resists further oxidation.

$$\text{R-CH}_2\text{OH (primary)} \rightarrow \text{R-CHO} \rightarrow \text{R-COOH}$$

**Compare the change in Mr for Y to P**

Aldehyde Y to acid P is simple oxidation, addition of one O atom.

$$M_r \text{ change} = +16$$

**Compare the change in Mr for Z to P**

Nitrile Z to acid P is acid hydrolysis. The $\text{-C}\equiv\text{N}$ group becomes $\text{-COOH}$.

$$\text{R-CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{R-COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$$
In mass terms, $\text{CN}$ mass 26 is replaced by $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ mass 45, so net change is $+19$, which is larger than $+16$ and larger than X to P ($+14$). So X is primary and the greatest Mr change is Z to P.

options.A: Half right but half wrong. X is correctly primary, but Y to P only adds one O atom (+16), which is less than the +19 change for hydrolysis of nitrile Z to P.
options.B: Correct on both counts. X must be primary to give acid P by oxidation, and Z to P involves replacing CN (26) with CO2H (45) for a net +19, greater than Y to P (+16) or X to P (+14).
options.C: Incorrect. A secondary alcohol oxidises to a ketone, not to a carboxylic acid, so X cannot be secondary. Y to P is also not the largest Mr change.
options.D: The second part is right, Z to P is the largest change, but the first part is wrong. A secondary alcohol cannot be converted to a carboxylic acid P, it stops at a ketone.
